Crow

Apsáalooke/Crow history in the northern Plains includes efforts to protect community life under reservation-era pressure. These readings pair a documented Plenty Coups study and historical treaty with Crow-led education and archival work at Little Big Horn College.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and context

The Crow Tribe, also known through the name Apsáalooke, has homelands in the northern plains.

Read the sources [5] National Park Service / Front Range Research Associates [6] Crow Tribal Legislature

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Apsáalooke-authored history, language, land and government. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation [2] crow-nsn.gov [3] crow-nsn.gov

03

A named leader, with differing interpretations

The NPS study presents Plenty Coups as a negotiator working to protect Crow land and political room for action. It also records different assessments of when he was generally recognized as principal chief. His home is one documented historic place; one leader’s experience does not represent every Crow viewpoint.

Read the sources [5] National Park Service / Front Range Research Associates

04

Reading the 1868 treaty

The edited treaty sets out reservation and agency provisions alongside compulsory schooling. Comparing those written terms with the later historical study helps frame questions about federal control and Crow responses. The document alone cannot show implementation or settle current rights and boundaries.

Read the sources [7] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; edited treaty text [5] National Park Service / Front Range Research Associates

05

Crow-led archives and access

Little Big Horn College’s proposal describes preserving recordings, improving language access and consulting Crow cultural scholars about appropriate presentation. It explains community and donor access controls. This is a record of work and aims described at that time, not permission to extract restricted material or proof that every proposed activity finished.

Read the sources [4] Little Big Horn College; public release by National Endowment for the Humanities

06

Education and community knowledge

The selected legislative findings identify the college as Crow-chartered and connect research with education, outreach and Crow culture and language. The 2017 resolution file carries a 2018 veto-override notice. It is a primary institutional record, not a complete account of current college policy.

Read the sources [6] Crow Tribal Legislature

Chief Plenty Coups Home — National Historic Landmark nomination, selected pages ↗

The 1998 property study offers a cited route into Plenty Coups’ political leadership and his home at Pryor. It is an outside historical interpretation, not a unanimous Crow account.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual61-page PDF: printed/PDFp4 house/setting; selectedpp19–23 leadership, negotiations and reservation-era pressures; p44 authors/date. Synthesis uses nonceremonial discussion pp20–23. No religious narratives, grave locations, maps or photographs republished.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public body inspected 2026-10-28 through normal HTTP200 retrieval, web reader or stated PDF pages. No bypass or outreach. Linked works, original records, audio and pictures were not automatically inspected or licensed. Prepared June4, 1998. Underlying manuscripts/interviews and all figures not inspected. Differing assessments of when he became principal chief remain uncertainty. Historical boundary descriptions are not present legal determinations.

Treaty with the Crows, 1868 — selected articles ↗

Edited treaty provisions offer a primary-document starting point for reservation-era policy, including agency buildings and compulsory schooling. They do not establish implementation or unanimous assent.

Scope: Actual HTML heading/preamble, Articles1–4 and7 read. Synthesis selects Article2 reservation, Article3 agency/school buildings and Article7 education provision.
